body:
What is environmental pollution?

Air, water and soil support life by supplying oxygen, water, nutrients and suitable conditions for living organisms. Human activities and natural events can change their composition. When an undesirable physical, chemical or biological change damages environmental quality or adversely affects living organisms, it is called environmental pollution.

A pollutant is a substance or agent that causes an undesirable change in environmental quality. Pollution may result from harmful chemicals, disease-causing microorganisms, suspended particles, excessive nutrients or physical changes such as an abnormal rise in water temperature.

A substance does not become harmful merely because it is present in the environment. Its concentration, location and effects matter. For example, nitrogen and phosphorus are essential plant nutrients, but excessive amounts entering a lake can cause harmful algal growth. Similarly, carbon dioxide is naturally present in air, while an increase in its atmospheric concentration contributes to global warming.

Major sources of pollutants

Pollutants arise from both natural processes and human activities. Their origin is important because identifying a source helps in selecting a suitable preventive measure.

SourceExamplesPossible pollution
TransportVehicle exhaust and road dustCarbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and particulate matter in air
IndustryFuel combustion and untreated effluentsGaseous emissions and chemical contamination of water
HouseholdsSewage, discarded cleaners and burning wasteWater contamination and smoke
AgricultureExcess fertilisers and pesticidesNutrient and chemical contamination of soil and water
Natural eventsForest fires, dust storms and volcanic activitySmoke, particles and gases in air

How pollution moves between air, water and soil

Air, water and soil are connected. Smoke particles released into air may settle on vegetation or soil. Rainwater can carry pollutants from roads and agricultural fields into streams. Some dissolved chemicals may seep through soil and reach groundwater. Pollutants entering soil may also be absorbed by plants and subsequently enter food chains.

These connections explain why the place where pollution is detected may differ from the place where it originated. A polluted river, for example, may receive contamination from settlements, industries or farms situated upstream.

Environmental and health effects

Different pollutants produce different effects. Air pollutants may irritate the respiratory system. Contaminated drinking water may spread infectious diseases or expose people to harmful chemicals. Soil pollutants may injure useful microorganisms, affect plant growth and contaminate food. Pollution can also damage buildings, reduce visibility and disturb aquatic ecosystems.

Pollution control involves preventing pollutants from being released, reducing their quantity, treating contaminated waste and preventing human exposure. Prevention at the source is generally preferable to dealing with contamination after it has spread.

Prelims focus

  • Pollution is an undesirable physical, chemical or biological change in environmental quality.
  • Pollutants may originate from natural events or human activities.
  • Air, water and soil pollution are interconnected because pollutants can move between them.
  • Excessive amounts of an otherwise useful substance can cause pollution.
  • Trap: Not every naturally occurring substance is always a pollutant; its concentration, location and effects are important.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 18, Pollution of Air and Water, sections 18.1, 18.2, 18.6 and 18.7, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 14, Natural Resources, sections 14.1–14.3, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 16, Environmental Issues, introduction and sections 16.1–16.4.]

pictures.caption: Everyday activities can introduce pollutants into air, water and soil.

pictures.alt: Particles settle on soil and plants; rain carries pollutants into streams; chemicals seep into groundwater; plant pollutants enter food chains.

title: Pollutants and Pollution: Meaning, Sources and Environmental Effects

body:
What makes air polluted?

Clean air is a mixture of gases, mainly nitrogen and oxygen, together with smaller quantities of other gases. Air pollution occurs when harmful gases, particles or other agents contaminate the atmosphere and adversely affect living organisms or materials.

Air pollutants may be released directly from a source or formed through reactions in the atmosphere. A primary pollutant is emitted directly, while a secondary pollutant forms after other substances react in air. Carbon monoxide emitted from a vehicle is an example of a primary pollutant. Ground-level ozone formed through atmospheric reactions is an example of a secondary pollutant.

Important air pollutants

PollutantCommon sourcesMain effects
Particulate matter (PM)Vehicle exhaust, road dust, construction, fuel and waste burningRespiratory and cardiovascular harm; reduced visibility
Carbon monoxide (CO)Incomplete combustion of fuelsReduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen
Sulphur dioxide (SO2)Combustion of sulphur-containing fuelsRespiratory irritation; formation of acid deposition
Nitrogen oxides (NOx)Vehicles, power plants and other high-temperature combustionRespiratory harm; contribution to acid rain and ozone formation
Ground-level ozone (O3)Forms from reactions involving nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds in sunlightBreathing difficulties and damage to vegetation

Particulate matter and particle size

Particulate matter consists of tiny solid particles and liquid droplets suspended in air. It includes dust, smoke, soot and other fine particles. Two widely used size categories are PM10, particles with an aerodynamic diameter of 10 micrometres or less, and PM2.5, particles with an aerodynamic diameter of 2.5 micrometres or less.

PM2.5 particles are smaller and can penetrate deeply into the respiratory system. Both PM10 and PM2.5 are important air-quality pollutants. The categories overlap: particles classified as PM2.5 also fall within the broader PM10 size range.

Carbon monoxide and incomplete combustion

When carbon-containing fuel does not burn completely, it can produce carbon monoxide. This gas is colourless and odourless. It binds strongly to haemoglobin in blood and reduces the amount of oxygen that blood can transport to body tissues. Therefore, exposure to carbon monoxide can be dangerous even when no smoke or unpleasant smell is noticed.

Incomplete combustion may occur in poorly ventilated spaces containing fuel-burning appliances. Vehicle exhaust and fuel-burning equipment are other possible sources. Good ventilation and properly maintained equipment help reduce exposure, but an unsafe combustion source must be corrected rather than merely masked by fragrance or ventilation.

Sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and combustion

Burning sulphur-containing coal or petroleum products releases sulphur dioxide. Nitrogen oxides can form during high-temperature combustion. These gases can irritate airways and may undergo further reactions in the atmosphere, producing substances associated with acid deposition and particulate pollution.

Smog and reduced visibility

The word smog originally combined smoke and fog. Polluted air may contain suspended particles and gases that reduce visibility. Modern usage also includes photochemical smog, which involves pollutants such as ground-level ozone formed in sunlight. The two situations are related to air pollution but are not chemically identical.

Consequences and elementary controls

Air pollution may cause coughing, irritation of the eyes and throat, worsening of asthma and other respiratory problems. Long-term exposure to some pollutants also increases the risk of cardiovascular and other diseases. Plants may suffer leaf injury or reduced growth, while dust and soot can dirty buildings and monuments.

Useful preventive measures include reducing unnecessary fuel combustion, avoiding open burning of waste, maintaining vehicles, using cleaner transport and preventing excessive dust emissions. Improving indoor ventilation and avoiding smoky cooking environments are also important.

Prelims focus

  • CO is mainly associated with incomplete combustion and reduced oxygen transport by blood.
  • SO2 and NOx are important precursors of acid rain.
  • PM10 refers to particles of 10 micrometres or less; PM2.5 refers to particles of 2.5 micrometres or less.
  • Ground-level ozone is a secondary pollutant.
  • Trap: PM2.5 is not a gas, and carbon monoxide is not the same substance as carbon dioxide.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 18, Pollution of Air and Water, sections 18.1–18.3, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 14, Natural Resources, section 14.1.4, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 16, Environmental Issues, section 16.1; World Health Organization, Air Pollution, sections on health effects and major pollutants, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: PM2.5 is within the PM10 size range; their diameter limits are 2.5 and 10 micrometres. Smaller particles can penetrate deeper into the respiratory system.
pictures.caption: Fine particles can penetrate more deeply into the respiratory system.

title: Air Pollution: Common Pollutants, Sources and Health Effects

body:
Ozone is a form of oxygen

Ordinary atmospheric oxygen exists mainly as molecules containing 2 oxygen atoms, represented by O2. Ozone contains 3 oxygen atoms per molecule and has the chemical formula O3. The effects of ozone depend strongly on where it is present in the atmosphere.

Stratospheric ozone protects life

The stratosphere lies above the troposphere, the atmospheric layer in which most weather occurs. Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs much of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation, particularly ultraviolet-B radiation. This protection reduces damage to the DNA and other biological molecules of living organisms.

Ozone in this region is continually formed and broken down through natural atmospheric processes. Under normal conditions, these processes maintain a dynamic balance. When ozone-destroying substances accelerate its breakdown, the protective layer becomes thinner.

Ground-level ozone is harmful

Ozone near Earth's surface is a harmful air pollutant. It can irritate the respiratory system, aggravate breathing problems and injure plant tissues.

Most ground-level ozone is not emitted directly from a vehicle or factory. It forms through sunlight-driven reactions involving nitrogen oxides (NOx) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs), which are carbon-containing chemicals that can enter air as gases from sources such as fuels and solvents. These reactions help produce photochemical smog.

Why the ozone layer becomes depleted

Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are compounds containing chlorine, fluorine and carbon. They were used in applications such as refrigerants and aerosol propellants. Many CFCs persist long enough to reach the stratosphere. Ultraviolet radiation can break them down, releasing chlorine atoms that participate in reactions destroying ozone.

Severe seasonal thinning of stratospheric ozone over Antarctica is commonly called the ozone hole. It does not mean that the atmosphere contains a literal empty opening. Rather, it describes an area where the concentration of protective ozone has become unusually low.

The Montreal Protocol

The Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer was agreed in 1987 and entered into force in 1989. Its central purpose is to control and phase out the production and consumption of specified ozone-depleting substances, including CFCs.

Ozone depletion is not the same as global warming

These are different environmental problems. Ozone depletion concerns the loss of protective stratospheric ozone and increased ultraviolet exposure. Global warming concerns the rise in Earth's average temperature caused by an enhanced greenhouse effect. Carbon dioxide and methane are important greenhouse gases, while CFCs are important ozone-depleting substances and can also contribute to greenhouse warming.

Stratospheric ozone is protective because it absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation. Tropospheric ozone is harmful because people and plants may be exposed to it near the surface. Both are chemically O3.

Prelims focus

  • Ozone has the chemical formula O3.
  • Stratospheric ozone absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation.
  • Ground-level ozone forms through reactions involving NOx, VOCs and sunlight.
  • CFCs contribute to depletion of stratospheric ozone.
  • The Montreal Protocol was agreed in 1987 and entered into force in 1989.
  • Trap: Ground-level ozone pollution and stratospheric ozone depletion are different problems.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 14, Natural Resources, section 14.5, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 16, Environmental Issues, section 16.7; United States Environmental Protection Agency, Ground-level Ozone Basics, sections on ozone formation and health effects, consulted 3 November 2026; United Nations Environment Programme, Ozone Secretariat, The Montreal Protocol, introduction and treaty history, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Ozone, O3, absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation in the stratosphere but harms breathing and plants near the ground; CFCs deplete stratospheric ozone.
pictures.caption: Ozone is protective high in the atmosphere but harmful near the ground.

title: Ozone: Protective Layer, Ground-Level Pollution and Ozone Depletion

body:
What is acid rain?

Rainwater is not necessarily neutral. Carbon dioxide naturally dissolves in atmospheric moisture and forms a weak acid, making ordinary rain slightly acidic. Under typical conditions, unpolluted rain has a pH of approximately 5.6.

Acid rain refers to precipitation made more acidic than this usual background condition, mainly because of acids formed from sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides in the atmosphere. Acidic substances can also reach Earth's surface without precipitation. The broader term acid deposition therefore includes both wet and dry deposition.

How sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides produce acids

Coal combustion, vehicle exhaust and industrial fuel burning can release sulphur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen oxides (NOx). In the atmosphere, these pollutants react with oxygen, water and other substances. Their reactions can produce sulphuric acid and nitric acid, which may dissolve in cloud droplets or occur in acidic particles.

  1. Fuel burning releases SO2 and NOx into the atmosphere.
  2. Atmospheric reactions convert these pollutants into acidic substances.
  3. Acids return to the surface in rain, snow or fog, or settle as dry particles and gases.
  4. Acid deposition affects water bodies, soils, vegetation and exposed structures.

Understanding the pH scale

The pH scale describes how acidic or alkaline an aqueous solution is. At ordinary conditions, a pH of 7 is neutral. A pH below 7 indicates acidity, while a pH above 7 indicates alkalinity. As pH decreases, acidity increases.

Ordinary rain commonly has a pH near 5.6. Acid rain may have a pH around 4.2 to 4.4, although actual values vary with place and conditions. A lower numerical pH therefore indicates greater acidity, not lower acidity.

Effects on water, soil, plants and buildings

Acid deposition can lower the pH of lakes and streams, making conditions unsuitable for some aquatic organisms. It can alter soil chemistry, contribute to the loss of useful nutrients and harm vegetation. The severity of these effects depends partly on the natural ability of soil and water to neutralise acids.

Acidic substances also react with some building materials. Limestone and marble contain calcium carbonate, which can be damaged by acids. Metals may also corrode more rapidly under acidic conditions.

The Taj Mahal example

The white marble of the Taj Mahal at Agra is a familiar Indian example of damage associated with air pollution. Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide emitted from industrial and other sources can contribute to acid formation. Acidic deposition may attack marble, while soot and other suspended particles can contribute to surface discoloration. School-level discussions sometimes call acid-related deterioration of marble marble cancer.

Carbon dioxide makes ordinary rain naturally slightly acidic, but sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides are the principal pollutants responsible for the acid-rain problem associated with fossil-fuel combustion. Acid rain should not be confused with either global warming or ozone depletion.

Prelims focus

  • SO2 and NOx are major precursors of acid rain.
  • Major acids involved are sulphuric acid and nitric acid.
  • Neutral water has a pH of approximately 7; ordinary rain is naturally slightly acidic, around pH 5.6.
  • Acid deposition includes wet and dry forms.
  • Acid rain can damage marble, including that used in the Taj Mahal.
  • Trap: A lower pH means greater acidity.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 18, Pollution of Air and Water, section 18.3, Case Study—The Taj Mahal, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 14, Natural Resources, section 14.1.4, 2018–19 edition; United States Environmental Protection Agency, What is Acid Rain?, sections What Causes Acid Rain? and Measuring Acid Rain, consulted 3 November 2026; United States Environmental Protection Agency, Effects of Acid Rain, sections on forests, aquatic environments and materials, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Fuel-burning emissions form acids in the atmosphere, then reach the ground by wet or dry deposition and affect water, soil, plants and marble.
pictures.caption: Sulphur and nitrogen oxides undergo atmospheric reactions before acidic substances reach the ground.

pictures.caption: Air pollution can damage marble monuments as well as living organisms.
